'## TOP-OF-DOC CALLOUT #0 — For the Trino-side `CREATE TABLE` DDL (target table), use r09's leading canonical worked example, NOT the Spark DDL forms in this resource\n\n> **This resource is the SPARK INGESTION guide.** Every `CREATE TABLE ... USING iceberg PARTITIONED BY (...) TBLPROPERTIES (...)` snippet below is **Spark SQL DDL** — submit via `spark-sql` or `spark.sql(...)`. **If you are creating the target Iceberg table from a Trino client (the Trino CLI, JDBC, the Trino UI, or any tool that speaks the Trino dialect), the Spark DDL forms in this resource will FAIL with a parse error.** Trino 467''s dialect requires PARENTHESES on parameterized types (`MAP(K, V)`, `ARRAY(T)`, `ROW(...)`), uses `WITH (partitioning = ARRAY[...])` inside the table-property clause instead of a trailing `PARTITIONED BY (...)`, uses `format_version` (integer, underscore) inside `WITH (...)` instead of `TBLPROPERTIES (''format-version''=''2'')`, and rejects `USING iceberg` entirely (the catalog name selects the connector).\n>\n> **For the canonical Trino-side `CREATE TABLE` DDL — both the worked example AND the DO-NOT-WRITE 7-row block listing every Spark-shaped DDL that parse-errors in Trino 467 — see** [resources/09-lakehouse-schema-design.md § LEADING CANONICAL WORKED EXAMPLE — Trino vs Spark DDL for a wide denormalized event table](09-lakehouse-schema-design.md). That section is the single source of truth for Trino 467 + Iceberg connector DDL; do not invent a parallel Trino-DDL form in this resource.\n>\n> **Quick decision rule:** if your engineer is going to type `CREATE TABLE iceberg.<schema>.<table>` into the Trino CLI before the Spark ingestion job runs, copy the Trino DDL block from r09. If your engineer is going to let the Spark ingestion job auto-create the table via `df.writeTo("iceberg.x.y").using("iceberg").create()` (or a Spark `CREATE TABLE` statement run from Spark), use the Spark DDL forms in this resource. The two paths produce the same on-disk Iceberg table; the syntax is engine-specific.'

When the cluster is\n-- eventually upgraded past 467, plan to switch to the table-procedure form in any\n-- scripts / runbooks. Until then, the CALL form above is the correct prod recipe.\n-- Do NOT use the Spark named-arg form (table => ..., snapshot_id => ...) from Trino either.'

The myths section contains 8 rows + a DO-NOT-WRITE 7-row block. Leading row (verbatim):

'| "Storage is essentially free on MinIO so we shouldn''t worry about TB growth." | **WRONG framing.** MinIO storage has zero *marginal* cost only once the disks, rack, power, cooling, and erasure-coding overhead are sunk costs you''ve already paid for. The honest all-in MinIO TCO is **$15–25/TB-month** when you include hardware amortization, EC overhead (default 4+2 = 1.5x raw), and ops/refresh allowance. For new capacity, use $20/TB-month as a budget anchor. The "free" framing is only valid when comparing marginal cost against the existing-cluster baseline. See `prod_info.md` for the on-prem mandate context. | [§ MinIO is NOT free — the real all-in $/TB-month estimate] |'

DO-NOT-WRITE block leading row (verbatim):
'| "Each Trino query on our stack costs $X" | Trino on-prem has NO per-query pricing | "Our Trino cluster has a fixed 24/7 cost of $Y; per-query marginal $ = 0" |'

The DO-NOT-WRITE block covers 7 chronic-fabrication patterns for cost on this on-prem stack: (1) per-query Trino pricing (Athena confusion), (2) Athena lift-and-shift as an action item (prod_info.md on-prem mandate hard-blocks this), (3) MinIO 'free' + snapshot retention 'doesn''t matter', (4) more workers as a cost lever (FALSE — on-prem fixed cluster cost), (5) FTE as a soft cost (FALSE — typically the LARGEST cost), (6) Iceberg snapshots 'tiny so keep forever', (7) AWS pricing pasted as action items.

The new section is placed BEFORE the leading worked example so a Haiku responder keyword-matching on 'cost', 'MinIO storage', 'Trino query cost', 'Athena cheaper', 'add more workers' lands here FIRST and is steered away from fabrication-prone framings. Existing leading worked example (storage-bloat 8TB→14TB) remains the primary actionable artifact; the myths table is the gatekeeper that prevents the responder from inventing per-query pricing or recommending an out-of-scope cloud migration.
